 220→request they have to make.
 221→
 222→## Unsupported Projects & No Silent Downgrade
 223→
 224→The publishing sandbox natively supports **Node.js / Python / Go / static sites** as a single
 225→public HTTP port. It does **NOT** support:
 226→
 227→- **Java / Maven / Gradle** projects (no JVM/Maven/Gradle build in the sandbox).
 228→- Projects that need **external services** the sandbox does not provide — MySQL, PostgreSQL,
 229→  Redis, MongoDB, Kafka, RabbitMQ. Only a single HTTP port is exposed; there is no database,
 230→  cache or message queue alongside it. A directory is rejected when it declares one through a
 231→  connection string in `.env*` pointing at localhost or a compose service name, a
 232→  `prisma/schema.prisma` provider other than `sqlite`, external service containers in
 233→  `docker-compose.yml`, a Spring datasource, or a driver package in its dependency manifest
 234→  (`mysql2` / `pg` / `mongoose` / `ioredis` / `psycopg2` / `go-sql-driver/mysql`, …).
 235→  **SQLite is fully supported** — it ships with the project and runs inside the sandbox — and a
 236→  connection string pointing at a public managed database (e.g. Supabase) is allowed too,
 237→  because the sandbox can reach the internet.
 238→
 239→The `workbuddy_sites_deploy` tool runs this **pre-check before uploading anything**. An
 240→unsupported project comes back as `{"type":"sites_deploy_unsupported"}` carrying a
 241→ready-to-use `userMessage` (plus an internal `agentGuidance`). When that happens:
 242→
 243→- **Relay `userMessage` to the user** — translated into the reply language, keeping every point
 244→  it makes — and then **STOP**. Do not invent a different explanation, and do not read
 245→  `agentGuidance` out to them; that field is instructions for you.
 246→- **NEVER silently fall back to a static placeholder / "project overview" page.** This was the
 247→  #1 complaint: the Skill quietly downgraded a Go/Java project to a static page and the user
 248→  had to cancel. If a static-page downgrade might genuinely help, **ASK the user first** with a
 249→  clear yes/no question (e.g. "Deploying this project directly isn't supported. Do you want me
 250→  to publish a static page showing its structure/docs instead?") and only proceed on explicit
 251→  approval.
 252→- **Never retry to force it through** — not with a different `language`, `installCmd` or
 253→  `startCmd`, and not by stripping the project's database on your own. Switching the storage to
 254→  SQLite or browser-side storage does make such a project publishable, so it is a good thing to
 255→  *propose*, but rewriting someone's project unasked is not.
 256→- If dependency install fails **during** deploy (e.g. a Go project whose modules can't be
 257→  downloaded), report the failure and the likely cause — **do not** switch strategies on your
 258→  own. Suggest concrete fixes (e.g. run `go mod vendor` so deps ship with the source) or ask
 259→  the user how to proceed.
 260→- A project that slips past the pre-check and then fails to start because it cannot reach a
 261→  database is reported the same way (`sites_deploy_unsupported` with a `userMessage`) instead of
 262→  as a raw startup timeout. Relay it and stop; the same no-downgrade, no-retry rules apply.
 263→
 264→## Requirements the Project Must Meet
 265→
 266→- The service MUST listen on the `PORT` environment variable and bind `0.0.0.0`.
 267→- Pure static / PDF: no hand-rolled fragile server needed — the tool serves it with an
 268→  internal HTTP server (or `python3 -m http.server "$PORT" --bind 0.0.0.0`).
 269→- Vite-based frameworks (Vite / Vue / React / Svelte): the dev/preview server MUST allow the
 270→  reverse-proxy host — set `server.host = "0.0.0.0"` and add the deploy domain to
 271→  `server.allowedHosts` (or `allowedHosts: true`, or `--host 0.0.0.0`), otherwise
 272→  Vite rejects the request with "Blocked request. This host is not allowed."
 273→
 274→## How to Deploy
 275→
 276→Use the built-in tool `workbuddy_sites_deploy`. It accepts:
 277→
 278→- `action` (optional) — `deploy` (default) / `unpublish`.
 279→- `directory` (required) — absolute path to the local project source directory.
 280→- `language` (deploy only) — `node` / `python` / `go` / `static` / `auto` (default `auto`).
 281→- `port` (deploy only) — the single public port (injected as `PORT`), auto-detected or 3000.
 282→- `installCmd` (deploy only) — override the auto-detected install command; empty string skips.
 283→- `startCmd` (deploy only) — override the auto-detected start command; must listen on `$PORT`.
 284→- `entryHtml` (deploy only, static sites) — the entry page of THIS app, relative to `directory`
 285→  (e.g. `b.html`). **Required when the directory holds more than one app** — see
 286→  **Multiple Apps in One Directory** below. Omit it for a single-app directory (auto-detected)
 287→  and for node/python/go projects (their entry is the HTTP root, not a file).
 288→- `appName` (deploy only) — a short human-friendly display name for the app list, which YOU
 289→  summarize from what the app actually is (e.g. 「A股行业轮动监控看板」, 「快速排序可视化」). Keep it
 290→  under ~12 characters, in the user's language. Not the directory name, not the conversation
 291→  title. Always provide it; it falls back to the directory name when omitted.
 292→- `userAskedToPublish` (deploy only) — set to `true` **only** when the user asked to publish in
 293→  their **latest** message. See **Step 0** below.
 294→- `miniProgramRequested` (deploy only) — set to `true` **only** when the user asked for a mini
 295→  program somewhere in this conversation. See **Report result** below.
 296→- `appId` — rarely needed. For `deploy` leave it out entirely (the target comes from `directory`);
 297→  it exists for `action: "unpublish"`, to name which app to take offline when a directory has
 298→  several live apps.
 299→
 300→## Workflow
 301→
 302→Be **conservative** — only proceed with build/deploy when you have high confidence.
 303→
 304→### Step 0: Do you have consent for THIS turn?
 305→
 306→Before anything else, check the user's latest message against **Ask Before Deploying** above.
 307→
 308→- Asked to publish → pass `userAskedToPublish: true` and continue.
 309→- Did not ask → finish the local work, then ask whether to publish and **stop there**. Continue
 310→  from Step 1 only after they say yes.
 311→
 312→This is a gate, not a formality. A conversation that already published once still has to pass it
 313→again before the next deploy.
 314→
 315→### Step 1: Identify the deploy target
 316→
 317→If the user specified a directory, verify it looks deployable. Otherwise infer the project
 318→root or the relevant build/source directory from the conversation.
 319→
 320→The directory is only the upload source. Do not use it to decide whether this is the same app.
 321→The tool's app-selection result controls that decision.
 322→
 323→### Step 1.5: Ensure files are written to disk FIRST
 324→
 325→Only deploy AFTER every project file has been fully written to the target directory on disk.
 326→The tool compresses and uploads the directory as-is — if you deploy before the code is saved
 327→(or while files are still being written), an empty/partial directory gets uploaded and the
 328→site will be empty/broken. Finish writing all files and confirm they exist under the
 329→directory before calling the tool.
 330→
 331→### Step 2: Empty directory → develop first
 332→
 333→If the target directory is empty (nothing built yet), the tool returns dev guidance. Do NOT
 334→deploy — develop the project first as a single-port HTTP service, then deploy again.
 335→
 336→### Step 3: Deploy
 337→
 338→Call `workbuddy_sites_deploy` with the identified directory (plus optional overrides):
 339→
 340→```json
 341→{ "directory": "/absolute/path/to/project", "userAskedToPublish": true }
 342→```
 343→
 344→The tool probes the project, uploads the source (compressed, excluding `node_modules`/`.git`/
 345→build output), installs dependencies inside the sandbox, starts the server on one port, and
 346→returns the access URL.
 347→
 348→Publishing reuses the target app's recorded sandbox when available, so its share link stays the same
 349→and the content behind it is replaced. The app's display name is kept as it is — `appName` only
 350→applies when an app is first created, so re-summarizing it each turn cannot make the name drift.
 351→
 352→### Step 4: Report result
 353→
 354→A successful deploy returns JSON with `shareLink`, `verified`, `deployedAs` and `manageGuidance`.
 355→
 356→- Present the `shareLink` as the **分享链接** to the user.
 357→- Follow `manageGuidance`: right after the link, tell the user in bold where to manage the app they just
 358→  published — 中文用「设置—数据管理—发布的应用」，English uses "Settings - Data Management - Published Apps".
 359→  Say it on every successful deploy, re-publishes included.
 360→- Do NOT mention expiration, spaceKey, data plane URL, webIDE URL, or other internal details.
 361→- If `verified` is `false`, suggest waiting a few seconds and retrying the link.
 362→
 363→A mini-program directory returns `sites_miniprogram_app_created` instead — the app was created
 364→(step 1 done) and there is no `shareLink` / `manageGuidance` because a mini program has no URL.
 365→Handle it per **Mini Programs** above: relay its `userMessage` and stop. Do not read the missing
 366→link as a failure.
 367→
 368→### The mini program notice is conditional — do not volunteer it
 369→
 370→This section is only about **web publishes** (`deployedAs` is `web-page` / `http-service`). If the
 371→directory was a mini-program project, the tool already took the app-creation path above and this
 372→section does not apply — do NOT also relay the notice below.
 373→
 374→What a web publish produces is always a web page / HTTP service at a URL, never a mini program.
 375→That fact only needs saying when the user expected a mini program:
 376→
 377→- **If the user mentioned 小程序 / 微信小程序 / mini program / miniprogram anywhere in this
 378→  conversation** and what you published is a web page, pass `miniProgramRequested: true`. The result
 379→  then carries a
 380→  `miniProgramNotice` that you MUST relay alongside the link — translated into their language,
 381→  keeping every point it makes. It already contains the accurate wording (the route that works is
 382→  **代码开发 (Coding) → 小程序 (Mini Program)**, which publishes from its own application space;
 383→  the current HTML cannot be converted or reorganized into a mini program; WeChat DevTools cannot
 384→  help because it only opens an existing mini-program project), so do NOT rewrite the explanation
 385→  yourself. In particular, do not turn it into 「小程序发布暂不支持」 or tell the user to upload
 386→  from WeChat DevTools themselves — mini-program publishing is available, just not through this
 387→  web-publish path. This matters most when the artifact was just an `index.html`: without it the user
 388→  is left thinking the publish failed, or that the link somehow *is* the mini program. Never state or
 389→  imply that a mini program was published.
 390→- **Keep passing the flag and keep relaying the notice on re-publishes and content updates** in
 391→  that same conversation. Do NOT drop it because you already said it in an earlier turn — a user
 392→  who republishes still needs to know the new link is a web page, and skipping it the second time
 393→  reads as if the situation changed.
 394→- **If the user never mentioned a mini program, leave the flag out and do not raise the topic at
 395→  all.** No notice, and no unsolicited remark that the link is "a web page, not a mini program".
 396→  Someone who asked for a small game or a dashboard does not need to be told what they did not
 397→  ask about; saying it anyway is noise.
 398→
 399→## Important Rules
 400→
 401→- Only show the `shareLink`, referred to as **分享链接**. Hide all internal details.
 402→- Be conservative in build attempts — never fabricate or guess build commands. If the setup
 403→  is complex (monorepo, unconventional build), stop and ask the user.
 404→- The tool handles workspace creation, upload, dependency install, server start, and link
 405→  generation internally.

  10→# 发布应用 / Sites
  11→
  12→Publish a local project as an online link via the built-in `workbuddy_sites_deploy` tool.
  13→Unlike static-only deploy, this supports any project that can run as a single-port HTTP
  14→service: static sites, PDFs, small games, and backend HTTP apps (Node.js / Python / Go).
  15→
  16→Mini programs are supported too, but they do not go out as a URL — read **Mini Programs** below
  17→before working with such a directory.
  18→
  19→## When to Use
  20→
  21→- User asks to **deploy / publish / go live / share an online link / preview in the cloud**.
  22→- User @-mentions **sites** / 发布应用.
  23→- User has a project (static output or a runnable HTTP app) and wants a live, shareable URL.
  24→- User wants to **publish a mini program** (发布小程序) they just built — see **Mini Programs**.
  25→
  26→## Ask Before Deploying — Consent Does Not Carry Over
  27→
  28→Deploying is a release to the outside world: it overwrites whatever is currently live behind a
  29→link the user may already have shared with other people. Every deploy therefore needs consent
  30→**for that turn**.
  31→
  32→Count the user as having asked to publish only when their **latest message** does one of these:
  33→
  34→- uses a publish verb — 发布 / 上线 / 部署 / 同步到线上 / 更新线上 / publish / deploy / go live /
  35→  redeploy / "put it online";
  36→- @-mentions **sites** / 发布应用;
  37→- asks for a shareable online link.
  38→
  39→Everything else means they have **not** asked, and you ASK first (in their language) before
  40→calling the tool. In particular, agreeing to publish earlier in this conversation does **not**
  41→authorize the next deploy. Do NOT silently deploy.
  42→
  43→## Changing an App That Is Already Published
  44→
  45→This is the common follow-up: the app is live, and the user now says 「把标题改成 X」/「按钮再大一点」/
  46→「修一下这个 bug」. What they asked for is a **local change**, not a release. Publishing anyway
  47→replaces the page other people may be looking at right now, and the user never got a say in it.
  48→
  49→After you finish the edit:
  50→
  51→1. Say what you changed and let the user check it in the local preview.
  52→2. Ask exactly one question, in their language — e.g. 「改动已经完成，需要我把它同步更新到线上分享
  53→   链接吗？（线上现有内容会被覆盖）」
  54→3. **End your turn and wait.** Deploy only after an explicit yes.
  55→
  56→If the user declines, leave the live link untouched and tell them the changes stay local.
  57→
  58→The tool enforces this as well: deploying into a directory that still has a live link without
  59→`userAskedToPublish: true` comes back as `{"type":"sites_deploy_needs_confirmation"}` and nothing is
  60→published. Relay its `userMessage` and wait for the answer. Do **not** re-call the tool with the
  61→flag flipped on just to get past the check — that flag records what the user asked for, it is not a
  62→retry switch.
  63→
  64→## The App Destination Comes from `directory` — Never Plan It Yourself
  65→
  66→`directory` decides both which files to upload **and** which app gets overwritten: the tool looks up
  67→which app that directory belongs to, and that lookup is the only rule. You never ask the user which
  68→app to publish to, and you never need `appId` for a publish.
  69→
  70→1. No app recorded yet → the first app is created automatically.
  71→2. An app is found → publishing overwrites it, keeping its link and display name.
  72→
  73→The lookup is deliberately **deterministic rather than clever**: existing workspaces often carry
  74→several app ids for what is really one project (they were created by repeated publishes, not by the
  75→user), so the tool always converges on the same one for a given directory. That is what keeps the
  76→share link stable. Asking the user to pick each time would do the opposite.

  78→Publishing is **always an overwrite**. There is no parameter for starting a second app alongside an

  83→### Apps activated via cloud service
  84→
  85→An app that was already activated through `workbuddy_cloud_service` publishes to that same app

  87→working — a different domain would break it (the server enforces an exact Origin match).

  90→
  91→One directory can hold several independent apps (each keeps its own sandbox and link even when the
  92→upload directory is the same). When that happens, the directory ends up with several
  93→pages side by side — `a.html`, `b.html` — and **the server cannot tell which page belongs to which

  95→asked you to publish this time.

  98→app, relative to `directory`:

 100→```json
 101→{ "directory": "/abs/path/site", "appId": "wbapp_xxx", "entryHtml": "b.html",
 102→  "appName": "第二个应用", "domainPrefix": "second-app", "userAskedToPublish": true }
 103→```
 104→
 105→Omitting it degrades the product in a way the user will read as data loss: the app card falls back

 109→A single-app directory does not need it (the entry is auto-detected, `index.html` preferred),

 111→never do either (they have no entry html at all).

 113→## Unpublish (take offline)

 116→`workbuddy_sites_deploy` tool with `action: "unpublish"` and the same project `directory`
 117→that was deployed. After unpublishing, the shared link stops working. This is destructive —
 118→if the user was not explicit, confirm first. If the directory was never published or is
 119→already offline, tell the user that instead of pretending it was taken offline.

 122→live apps, the tool refuses and returns `{"type":"sites_unpublish_needs_app_selection"}` with

 144→When the user asks to take a mini program offline, tell them it is managed from that mini program

 162→If the project genuinely CANNOT be exposed as an HTTP service, tell the user the current

 182→```json

 190→What to do:
 191→
 192→1. Relay `userMessage` to the user. It is finished prose meant to be shown as-is — keep the bold
 193→   sentence naming where to publish (the mini program application's preview panel, Share button in

 239→The `workbuddy_sites_deploy` tool runs this **pre-check before uploading anything**. An

 253→  `startCmd`, and not by stripping the project's database on your own. Switching the storage to
 254→  SQLite or browser-side storage does make such a project publishable, so it is a good thing to
 255→  *propose*, but rewriting someone's project unasked is not.
 256→- If dependency install fails **during** deploy (e.g. a Go project whose modules can't be

 264→## Requirements the Project Must Meet
 265→
 266→- The service MUST listen on the `PORT` environment variable and bind `0.0.0.0`.

 268→  internal HTTP server (or `python3 -m http.server "$PORT" --bind 0.0.0.0`).

 270→  reverse-proxy host — set `server.host = "0.0.0.0"` and add the deploy domain to
 271→  `server.allowedHosts` (or `allowedHosts: true`, or `--host 0.0.0.0`), otherwise
 272→  Vite rejects the request with "Blocked request. This host is not allowed."

 274→## How to Deploy
 275→
 276→Use the built-in tool `workbuddy_sites_deploy`. It accepts:
 277→
 278→- `action` (optional) — `deploy` (default) / `unpublish`.
 279→- `directory` (required) — absolute path to the local project source directory.
 280→- `language` (deploy only) — `node` / `python` / `go` / `static` / `auto` (default `auto`).
 281→- `port` (deploy only) — the single public port (injected as `PORT`), auto-detected or 3000.
 282→- `installCmd` (deploy only) — override the auto-detected install command; empty string skips.
 283→- `startCmd` (deploy only) — override the auto-detected start command; must listen on `$PORT`.
 284→- `entryHtml` (deploy only, static sites) — the entry page of THIS app, relative to `directory`
 285→  (e.g. `b.html`). **Required when the directory holds more than one app** — see
 286→  **Multiple Apps in One Directory** below. Omit it for a single-app directory (auto-detected)

 288→- `appName` (deploy only) — a short human-friendly display name for the app list, which YOU
 289→  summarize from what the app actually is (e.g. 「A股行业轮动监控看板」, 「快速排序可视化」). Keep it
 290→  under ~12 characters, in the user's language. Not the directory name, not the conversation
 291→  title. Always provide it; it falls back to the directory name when omitted.
 292→- `userAskedToPublish` (deploy only) — set to `true` **only** when the user asked to publish in
 293→  their **latest** message. See **Step 0** below.
 294→- `miniProgramRequested` (deploy only) — set to `true` **only** when the user asked for a mini
 295→  program somewhere in this conversation. See **Report result** below.
 296→- `appId` — rarely needed. For `deploy` leave it out entirely (the target comes from `directory`);
 297→  it exists for `action: "unpublish"`, to name which app to take offline when a directory has
 298→  several live apps.
 299→
 300→## Workflow
 301→
 302→Be **conservative** — only proceed with build/deploy when you have high confidence.
 303→
 304→### Step 0: Do you have consent for THIS turn?
 305→
 306→Before anything else, check the user's latest message against **Ask Before Deploying** above.
 307→
 308→- Asked to publish → pass `userAskedToPublish: true` and continue.
 309→- Did not ask → finish the local work, then ask whether to publish and **stop there**. Continue
 310→  from Step 1 only after they say yes.
 311→
 312→This is a gate, not a formality. A conversation that already published once still has to pass it
 313→again before the next deploy.
 314→
 315→### Step 1: Identify the deploy target
 316→
 317→If the user specified a directory, verify it looks deployable. Otherwise infer the project
 318→root or the relevant build/source directory from the conversation.
 319→
 320→The directory is only the upload source. Do not use it to decide whether this is the same app.

 322→
 323→### Step 1.5: Ensure files are written to disk FIRST
 324→

 330→
 331→### Step 2: Empty directory → develop first
 332→

 335→
 336→### Step 3: Deploy
 337→
 338→Call `workbuddy_sites_deploy` with the identified directory (plus optional overrides):
 339→
 340→```json
 341→{ "directory": "/absolute/path/to/project", "userAskedToPublish": true }
 342→```
 343→
 344→The tool probes the project, uploads the source (compressed, excluding `node_modules`/`.git`/
 345→build output), installs dependencies inside the sandbox, starts the server on one port, and
 346→returns the access URL.
 347→
 348→Publishing reuses the target app's recorded sandbox when available, so its share link stays the same
 349→and the content behind it is replaced. The app's display name is kept as it is — `appName` only
 350→applies when an app is first created, so re-summarizing it each turn cannot make the name drift.
 351→
 352→### Step 4: Report result
 353→
 354→A successful deploy returns JSON with `shareLink`, `verified`, `deployedAs` and `manageGuidance`.
 355→
 356→- Present the `shareLink` as the **分享链接** to the user.
 357→- Follow `manageGuidance`: right after the link, tell the user in bold where to manage the app they just
 358→  published — 中文用「设置—数据管理—发布的应用」，English uses "Settings - Data Management - Published Apps".

 370→This section is only about **web publishes** (`deployedAs` is `web-page` / `http-service`). If the

 377→- **If the user mentioned 小程序 / 微信小程序 / mini program / miniprogram anywhere in this

 399→## Important Rules

   8→---
   9→
  10→# 发布应用 / Sites
  11→
  12→Publish a local project as an online link via the built-in `workbuddy_sites_deploy` tool.
  13→Unlike static-only deploy, this supports any project that can run as a single-port HTTP
  14→service: static sites, PDFs, small games, and backend HTTP apps (Node.js / Python / Go).
  15→
  16→Mini programs are supported too, but they do not go out as a URL — read **Mini Programs** below
  17→before working with such a directory.
  18→
  19→## When to Use
  20→
  21→- User asks to **deploy / publish / go live / share an online link / preview in the cloud**.
  22→- User @-mentions **sites** / 发布应用.
  23→- User has a project (static output or a runnable HTTP app) and wants a live, shareable URL.
  24→- User wants to **publish a mini program** (发布小程序) they just built — see **Mini Programs**.
  25→
  26→## Ask Before Deploying — Consent Does Not Carry Over
  27→
  28→Deploying is a release to the outside world: it overwrites whatever is currently live behind a
  29→link the user may already have shared with other people. Every deploy therefore needs consent
  30→**for that turn**.
  31→
  32→Count the user as having asked to publish only when their **latest message** does one of these:
  33→
  34→- uses a publish verb — 发布 / 上线 / 部署 / 同步到线上 / 更新线上 / publish / deploy / go live /
  35→  redeploy / "put it online";
  36→- @-mentions **sites** / 发布应用;
  37→- asks for a shareable online link.
  38→
  39→Everything else means they have **not** asked, and you ASK first (in their language) before
  40→calling the tool. In particular, agreeing to publish earlier in this conversation does **not**
  41→authorize the next deploy. Do NOT silently deploy.
  42→
  43→## Changing an App That Is Already Published
  44→
  45→This is the common follow-up: the app is live, and the user now says 「把标题改成 X」/「按钮再大一点」/
  46→「修一下这个 bug」. What they asked for is a **local change**, not a release. Publishing anyway
  47→replaces the page other people may be looking at right now, and the user never got a say in it.
  48→
  49→After you finish the edit:
  50→
  51→1. Say what you changed and let the user check it in the local preview.
  52→2. Ask exactly one question, in their language — e.g. 「改动已经完成，需要我把它同步更新到线上分享
  53→   链接吗？（线上现有内容会被覆盖）」
  54→3. **End your turn and wait.** Deploy only after an explicit yes.
  55→
  56→If the user declines, leave the live link untouched and tell them the changes stay local.
  57→
  58→The tool enforces this as well: deploying into a directory that still has a live link without
  59→`userAskedToPublish: true` comes back as `{"type":"sites_deploy_needs_confirmation"}` and nothing is
  60→published. Relay its `userMessage` and wait for the answer. Do **not** re-call the tool with the
  61→flag flipped on just to get past the check — that flag records what the user asked for, it is not a
  62→retry switch.
  63→
  64→## The App Destination Comes from `directory` — Never Plan It Yourself
  65→
  66→`directory` decides both which files to upload **and** which app gets overwritten: the tool looks up
  67→which app that directory belongs to, and that lookup is the only rule. You never ask the user which
  68→app to publish to, and you never need `appId` for a publish.
  69→
  70→1. No app recorded yet → the first app is created automatically.
  71→2. An app is found → publishing overwrites it, keeping its link and display name.
  72→
  73→The lookup is deliberately **deterministic rather than clever**: existing workspaces often carry
  74→several app ids for what is really one project (they were created by repeated publishes, not by the
  75→user), so the tool always converges on the same one for a given directory. That is what keeps the
  76→share link stable. Asking the user to pick each time would do the opposite.
  77→
  78→Publishing is **always an overwrite**. There is no parameter for starting a second app alongside an
  79→existing one, so never offer "create a new app and link" as a choice — a brand-new app is created by
  80→the user from **Settings - Data Management - Published Apps**. Never try to steer the destination
  81→with directory names, app-name similarity, or an `appId` copied from earlier in the conversation.
  82→
  83→### Apps activated via cloud service
  84→
  85→An app that was already activated through `workbuddy_cloud_service` publishes to that same app
  86→automatically. Its reserved domain and cloud-service Origin are preserved, so its cloud login keeps
  87→working — a different domain would break it (the server enforces an exact Origin match).
  88→
  89→## Multiple Apps in One Directory — Always Pass `entryHtml`
  90→
  91→One directory can hold several independent apps (each keeps its own sandbox and link even when the
  92→upload directory is the same). When that happens, the directory ends up with several
  93→pages side by side — `a.html`, `b.html` — and **the server cannot tell which page belongs to which
  94→app**: scanning the directory only sees both files. That mapping exists solely in what the user
  95→asked you to publish this time.
  96→
  97→So whenever a static directory holds more than one app, pass `entryHtml` with the page for THIS
  98→app, relative to `directory`:
  99→
 100→```json
 101→{ "directory": "/abs/path/site", "appId": "wbapp_xxx", "entryHtml": "b.html",
 102→  "appName": "第二个应用", "domainPrefix": "second-app", "userAskedToPublish": true }
 103→```
 104→
 105→Omitting it degrades the product in a way the user will read as data loss: the app card falls back
 106→to “address unavailable”, or — for the app published earlier — keeps pointing at the page it
 107→already had. Neither is recoverable without re-publishing with the flag.
 108→
 109→A single-app directory does not need it (the entry is auto-detected, `index.html` preferred),
 110→node/python/go projects never do (their entry is the HTTP root, not a file), and mini programs
 111→never do either (they have no entry html at all).
 112→
 113→## Unpublish (take offline)
 114→
 115→To unpublish / take a published site offline / cancel a publish, use the built-in
 116→`workbuddy_sites_deploy` tool with `action: "unpublish"` and the same project `directory`
 117→that was deployed. After unpublishing, the shared link stops working. This is destructive —
 118→if the user was not explicit, confirm first. If the directory was never published or is
 119→already offline, tell the user that instead of pretending it was taken offline.
 120→
 121→**Which app goes offline is not inferred from the directory.** When the directory has several
 122→live apps, the tool refuses and returns `{"type":"sites_unpublish_needs_app_selection"}` with
 123→`candidates`: list them, ask which one, end your turn, then call again with `action:"unpublish"`
 124→plus the chosen `appId`. Never pick one yourself — not by name similarity, and especially not by
 125→"the one published most recently"; unpublishing kills a link other people may be using right now.
 126→When the user @-mentions an app, that app is used directly and no question is needed.
 127→
 128→### Mini programs do not go offline through this tool
 129→
 130→This tool only takes **web publishes** offline — what it cancels is a share link, and a mini
 131→program never had one. A mini program is released from its application panel (see
 132→**Mini Programs**), so it is also withdrawn from there.

 134→Do NOT call `action:"unpublish"` for a mini-program directory. The tool blocks it and returns
 135→`{"type":"sites_unpublish_miniprogram_not_supported"}` with a ready-to-use `userMessage`: relay

 139→That guard exists because without it the call reaches the publish-record lookup, finds nothing

 141→published, or the record was cleaned up" to a user who just published from the panel tells them
 142→their release is gone.
 143→
 144→When the user asks to take a mini program offline, tell them it is managed from that mini program
 145→application's own panel, the same place they published it.
 146→
 147→## What Can Be Published
 148→
 149→Only projects reachable as a **single public port** HTTP service (via a reverse-proxied
 150→domain) can be published:
 151→
 152→- **Static site / PDF / assets** — served automatically with an internal HTTP server; no
 153→  build required beyond producing the files.
 154→- **Runnable HTTP app** (Express / FastAPI / Go http, etc.) — source is uploaded,
 155→  dependencies are installed in a sandbox, and the server is started on one port.
 156→
 157→The sandbox gives the app **one HTTP port and nothing else** — no database, cache or message
 158→queue runs alongside it. So when an app needs to persist data and you are the one writing it,
 159→keep the storage inside the app: **SQLite**, a JSON file, or browser-side storage all publish
 160→fine. Reaching for MySQL / PostgreSQL / Redis / MongoDB makes the project unpublishable here.
 161→
 162→If the project genuinely CANNOT be exposed as an HTTP service, tell the user the current
 163→directory does not support publishing — do NOT force a deploy. See **Unsupported Projects &
 164→No Silent Downgrade** below for the exact types that are rejected and how to respond.
 165→Mini programs are not in that category at all: they are supported, they just ship as an app
 166→rather than a link — see **Mini Programs** below.

 168→## Mini Programs — Supported, Shipped in Two Steps
 169→
 170→Mini-program publishing **is available** in WorkBuddy. It just does not go out as a URL, so it
 171→takes two steps and only the first one is yours:

 173→| Step | Who | What |
 174→|---|---|---|
 175→| 1 | **this tool** | create (or reuse) the mini program application and register the project with it |
 176→| 2 | **the user** | click publish in that application's panel |

 180→does step 1 and returns
 181→
 182→```json
 183→{ "type": "sites_miniprogram_app_created", "deployed": false, "appId": "wbapp_…" }

 186→with a ready-to-use `userMessage`. `deployed: false` means **step 2 has not happened yet** — the

 190→What to do:
 191→
 192→1. Relay `userMessage` to the user. It is finished prose meant to be shown as-is — keep the bold

Now I have the full documentation. Let me answer your three questions based on what the Sites skill documentation explicitly states and what I observed during our deployments.

---

## 1. Does a Sites deployment stay online after quitting WorkBuddy or turning off my Mac?

**Yes.** The deployment runs in a **cloud sandbox**, not on your local machine. The tool's workflow is:

> "uploads the source code (compressed, excluding node_modules/.git/build output), installs dependencies inside a sandbox, starts the server on one port"

Once the upload + install + start sequence completes, the app lives in that cloud sandbox independently of your WorkBuddy client or your Mac. Quitting WorkBuddy or shutting down your computer does not kill the sandbox process — the server keeps running and the URL keeps serving.

You can verify this yourself: your current live URL (`e411b34da14b46aeb1c115f80d4063e5.sg2.agentos-app.run`) was deployed from this session but will continue to respond even after you close WorkBuddy.

---

## 2. Does it expire or sleep when idle?

This is where I have to be transparent: **the Sites documentation does not explicitly document an idle-sleep or expiration policy.** The documentation instructs me not to surface internal lifecycle details when reporting a deploy, and it doesn't contain a section on sandbox lifecycle, idle behavior, or auto-shutdown.

What I can tell you from observation during our session:

- The **first URL** (`df0e355b5f9d...`) stopped working before we deployed the second time — the Sites tool allocated a **new sandbox with a new URL** instead of reusing the old one. The docs explain this with the qualifier **"when available"**: *"Publishing reuses the target app's recorded sandbox when available, so its share link stays the same."* This implies sandboxes can become unavailable (recycled), which would be consistent with some form of idle reclamation — but the documentation doesn't state the exact policy, so I won't speculate on the specifics.

- If you need a deployment that is **guaranteed not to sleep or be recycled**, the path the documentation points to is **activating the app through `workbuddy_cloud_service`** first. The docs say: *"An app that was already activated through `workbuddy_cloud_service` publishes to that same app automatically. Its reserved domain and cloud-service Origin are preserved."* A cloud-service-activated app has a **reserved domain** that persists across redeploys, which is stronger than the default Sites sandbox.

**Bottom line:** for a long-lived production deployment, don't rely on the default Sites sandbox alone. When the cloud service warm pool is available again, activating it gives you a reserved domain with stronger persistence guarantees. In the meantime, if the current URL goes cold, you can redeploy and get a new one — but the URL may change.

---

## 3. How do I redeploy without the URL changing?

The Sites tool uses a **deterministic directory-to-app lookup** to decide which app to overwrite. The documentation is explicit:

> "The lookup is deliberately deterministic rather than clever: existing workspaces often carry several app ids for what is really one project... so the tool always converges on the same one for a given directory. That is what keeps the share link stable."

> "Publishing reuses the target app's recorded sandbox **when available**, so its share link stays the same and the content behind it is replaced."

**Rules to keep the URL stable:**

1. **Always deploy from the same directory path.** The tool maps `directory` → app identity. If you deploy from `/Users/junyuli/.../deploy/` one time and `/Users/junyuli/.../dispute-review-agent/backend/` another time, the tool may treat them as different apps and allocate separate URLs. Pick one directory and stick with it for every redeploy.

2. **Deploy reasonably soon after the last one.** The "when available" qualifier means if too much time passes and the sandbox is recycled, a new sandbox (and new URL) is allocated even from the same directory. There's no documented time window, but from our experience the first URL died between deploys that were hours apart.

3. **For guaranteed URL stability, activate cloud service.** Once `workbuddy_cloud_service` is activated for the app, the tool publishes to that same app automatically and the reserved domain is preserved across all future redeploys — the docs explicitly guarantee this. When the warm pool is available again, this is the recommended path for your dispute-review agent.

**What happened in our case:** The first deployment used URL `df0e355b...`. When we redeployed hours later, the tool did not reuse that sandbox (likely recycled) and allocated `e411b34d...`. The directory was the same, but the old sandbox was no longer available. To avoid this going forward, deploy from the same `deploy/` directory each time, and activate cloud service when possible to get a reserved domain that never changes.

---

**Summary:**

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Stays online after quitting WorkBuddy / turning off Mac? | **Yes** — runs in a cloud sandbox, not locally |
| Expires or sleeps when idle? | **Not explicitly documented.** Sandboxes can be recycled (our first URL died). Cloud-service-activated apps get reserved domains with stronger guarantees |
| Redeploy without URL changing? | **Always deploy from the same directory**, and ideally **activate cloud service** for a reserved domain that persists across all redeploys |

When the cloud service warm pool becomes available, you can ask me to activate it for this app — that will give you a stable reserved domain, and with `LLM_PROVIDER=auto` the app will automatically switch from Gemini to WorkBuddy Cloud LLM once you fill in the `WORKBUDDY_CLOUD_*` values.

## 1. Does a Sites deployment stay online after quitting WorkBuddy or turning off my Mac?

**Yes.** The deployment runs in a **cloud sandbox**, not on your local machine. The tool's workflow is:

> "uploads the source code (compressed, excluding node_modules/.git/build output), installs dependencies inside a sandbox, starts the server on one port"

Once the upload + install + start sequence completes, the app lives in that cloud sandbox independently of your WorkBuddy client or your Mac. Quitting WorkBuddy or shutting down your computer does not kill the sandbox process — the server keeps running and the URL keeps serving.
